questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To find the place interesting, to have never been there before.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy as you are given mobility coordinators and such. The hard part was coordinating my home and receiving institution regarding deadlines and dates and such. For instance, I had to "pretend" to choose courses in advance so I could fill out the forms for my home university, even though the course catalogue for the receiving institution was only released a few weeks before the start of the semester. It is possible but it is a little messy.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: In the abovementioned case, my mobility coordinator was able to work with me and submitted my forms even with the incorrect courses listed so that I could get my Erasmus grant in time and so on. We worked out that I could submit things again with the correct courses when it was possible.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Quite easy as I found a dorm. It is very different from the dorms in Denmark though, they are not at all as social and clean.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would recommend finding a place to live in a shared house with other people instead if you are looking for being social with roommates and cleaner living. The dorm floor I was on became quite social after a little while so it is possible to create an environment like this, but I know of some others in the same building where they did not even say hello, so it's also a matter of luck!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You choose from a course catalogue and get spaces according to how many spots are available. There is also a dropping period which made it easier to figure out how to do the points that were needed for the home uni as well as host uni (at least half of your ECTS has to be in your home department).

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much but I and others from my home university coordinated with each other which helped a lot.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Fine, although we ended up with a bigger course load than we are used to.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Coordinate with other people if possible - it makes it less stressful. Also please note that Vienna differentiates between "VO" (lectures) and "SE" (seminars). Seminars expect you to participate actively and hand in assignments during the semester, etc.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Quite different - much more "class teaching" with active participation and assignments during the semester. The classes varied a lot though, as the teachers had a lot of impact on how it was run. One teacher liked to sit in a circle of chairs and one preferred to talk at the white boards, etc.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Political Sociology (VO), Urban Sociology (VO), Imagining Mobility (SE), Borders and Mobility (SE), What is Power (SE), Digital Visuality and Popular Culture (SE), Writing and Representing in Science and Technology Studies (SE)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend any STS courses for specifically sociology students as we do not really go into that at ucph - in Vienna they are really into it and I found it very interesting and opened my eyes for some cool topics and theories I think I will bring with me home as well. The STS courses I took were Borders and Mobility and Writing and Representing in STS. Borders and Mobility was particularly interesting and I really liked my lecturer, Fredy Gamez.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The registration forms sometimes cost mony. I had to pay 30 euro for a form for registrating for living in Vienna.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries were less expensive than I thought. Also the public transport for a trip here and there was very inexpensive - I rented a swapfiets bike however instead and only opted for the public transport every once in a while.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were student bars at my department but it was not very easy to be there if you didn't speak german I found. I think there are clubs for different things, but to be honest, I didn't really investigate these opportunities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club if possible? :D

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go see every museum possible and go on small trips to picturesque spots! Kahlenberg and Schönbrunn are good examples - they are close by the city but offer something the downtown areas don't :D

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Talk to other exchange students in your classes or where you live. And go to "travel bars", a lot of exchange students/travellers hang out here.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There are SO many registration processes and a lot of it includes showing up at some office in person and receiving a piece of PAPER with a physical signature/stamp. I and others from the same home uni found this very confusing to navigate. For instance, you have to register yourself as a citizen living in Vienna upon three days of arrival and show up at office 1 and fill out a form which will be stamped and signed, then you take this piece of paper and call office 2 (in a different part of town) and get a time slot a month in advance to register there. Then you are registered in Vienna. Then you have to DEregister when leaving, also with a time slot and so on. I know of some who just skipped this process, but I also heard you get a fine if you do.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Very beautiful city with so much going on. There are small festivals for art/music/etc., exhibitions and Wiener-concerts all the time. Lots of orchestra concerts, and much of the time there are free ones!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Apply for grants if eligible, they are a lifesaver. I applied to maybe 4 but only got one, so do research on that before travelling and make sure you exhaust your possiblities in this area.
Don't get overwhelmed by all the processes of registration and paperwork - it seems impossible at times but it works out. 
See as many cultural things as possible, there are plenty of options! Make time for it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I recommend getting a bike if you are comfortable biking. The lanes are NOT like in Copenhagen - traffic is much more chaotic and cars are not at all as aware of you, but it is a great way to get to know the city and how it connects and to move around more freely! I rented at Swapfiets which was very easy and that way you know it is in good condition.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know a foreign city that I will be able to return to and know in a different way than a tourist ever could!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Figuring out all the paperwork and deadlines and matching it with my home university.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
